edits.english: The mishna states: If the court of one of the tribes issued a ruling, Rabbi Yehuda says that that tribe is liable to bring a bull and the rest of all the tribes are exempt. A dilemma was raised before the Sages: According to Rabbi Yehuda, in the case of one tribe that performed a transgression on the basis of the ruling of the High Court, are the other tribes liable to bring a bull or not? The Gemara elaborates: Do we say that it is specifically in a case where seven tribes sinned that other tribes each bring a bull together with them because there is a majority of the tribes that sinned, but in a case where only one tribe sinned, where there is no majority of the tribes that sinned, they do not? Or perhaps it is no different, and the other tribes are drawn after even one tribe.
But one tribe, where there is no majority, no - And the same applies to two or three tribes.

We learned in the mishna that if the court of one of the tribes issued a ruling, Rabbi Yehuda says that that tribe brings a bull and the rest of the tribes are exempt. A dilemma was raised before them [the students]: According to Rabbi Yehuda, in the case of one tribe that sinned on the basis of the ruling of the High Court, do they bring a bull also the other tribes or not? And the sides of the question: Do we say: Specifically when seven tribes sinned, the law is that the other tribes bring a bull with them, because there is a majority of tribes, but when one tribe sinned, where there is no majority of tribes - no, or perhaps it is no different! And even one tribe draws the others!

Rashi wrote that it is not specifically one tribe, but the same applies if a minority of tribes sinned; there is a discussion about what the law would be, whether they draw the other tribes with them or not.

Seven tribes are the ones that bring etc. - According to Rabbi Yehuda, who said in the baraita above, even two tribes, this is what he meant to ask. But for two tribes, no; rather, it is from the mishna that he asks, which deals with seven tribes.
Rabbi Shimon requires eight - A bull for each and every tribe and a bull for the court.
If on the ruling of its court, Rabbi Shimon does not accept it - For it does not make the term 'congregation' superfluous for the ruling of its court.

They propose a solution: Come and hear [come and hear from a baraita]: What do they bring? One bull; Rabbi Shimon says: Two bulls. And we clarify: What are we dealing with [what are we dealing with] in this baraita? If you say [if you say] in a case where seven tribes sinned, then according to Rabbi Shimon, eight [eight bulls] are needed, which are one for each tribe and one more for the court! Rather, it must be said that one tribe sinned. And we clarify: In what [in what]? That is, according to whom did that tribe act? If [if] you say they sinned on the ruling of its court, Rabbi Shimon does not accept it [does not have it, does not accept] the reasoning that the ruling of a tribal court obligates a bull! Rather, is it not [is it not] necessary to say that the intention is that they acted on the ruling of the High Court.

Rashi explains that we know that Rabbi Shimon does not accept the reasoning that one tribe brings an offering based on its court's ruling, because according to the way he interprets the verses, there is no superfluous word "congregation" that would come to teach this. And the Rosh believes that this is not a proof, because they brought this midrashic opinion only because they knew that this was Rabbi Shimon's opinion. Rather, he believes (as the Gemara states later) that the anonymous mishna stated at the end, which says that offerings are only brought based on the ruling of the High Court, is Rabbi Shimon's opinion, and he is the one who disputes Rabbi Yehuda on this.
Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda? - And it teaches: What do they bring? One bull. This implies that the other tribes do not bring an offering with it.

And we further clarify: And who is the first tanna [and who is the first tanna] who says that they bring one bull? If you say [if you say] that Rabbi Meir is he, behold, he requires a majority [he requires a majority] and one tribe is not enough for him! Rather, is it not [is it not] the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, and here it is a case where one tribe sinned and even he only obligates one bull, and the other tribes do not bring an offering.

They say: What are we dealing with here, etc.? - And the first tanna is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. And Rabbi Shimon, who said two bulls, holds that a bull for each and every tribe, because one tribe is called a congregation, such as when seven tribes sinned and they are a majority of the congregation. For when there is a majority in terms of people and a majority in terms of tribes, then he brings a bull for each and every tribe and a bull for the court. But where there are six and they are a majority, or seven and they are not a majority, since there is not a majority in terms of people and a majority in terms of tribes, they are considered like one tribe, and they bring one bull and a bull for the court.

They reject this proof: They say, it is possible to explain this baraita in another way: What are we dealing with here? For example, where six tribes sinned and they are a majority of the congregation, and it is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that in this case they bring a bull. As it is taught in a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir: If six tribes sinned and they are a majority of the congregation, or seven tribes, even though they are not a majority of the congregation - they bring a bull.

For example, where six tribes sinned and they are a majority etc. - It is a wonder, if so, what is the reason of Rabbi Shimon, who only obligates one bull? We have not found that he disputes Rabbi Yehuda, except that he also requires a bull for the court. But he does agree with Rabbi Yehuda that one tribe is called a congregation.

Come and hear [come and hear] a solution to the problem from another baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says: A tribe that acted on the ruling of its court - that tribe is liable and all the other tribes are exempt, and on the ruling of the High Court - even the other tribes are liable. And they conclude: Indeed, learn from it [learn from here] that this is Rabbi Yehuda's opinion in this case.

Rav Ashi said: The language of the mishna is also precise in support of that conclusion, as it teaches: If the court of one of the tribes issued an erroneous ruling and the majority of that tribe performed a transgression on the basis of its ruling, that tribe is liable to bring an offering and all the rest of the tribes are exempt. Rav Ashi explains: Why do I need the tanna to teach: And the rest of the tribes are exempt? Didn’t the tanna already teach: That tribe is liable? And since the tanna teaches: That tribe is liable, we know automatically that the rest of the tribes are exempt. Rather, this tanna is teaching us that it is specifically in a case where the tribe performed an unwitting transgression on the basis of its tribal court's ruling that the rest of the tribes are exempt; but in a case where the tribe performed an unwitting transgression on the basis of the High Court's ruling, even the rest of the tribes are liable. The Gemara concludes: Learn from the mishna that this is Rabbi Yehuda’s opinion.

Rav Ashi said: Our mishna is also precise [our mishna is also precise] according to this view, as it teaches [that it taught in it]: And that tribe acted according to their ruling - that tribe is liable and all the other tribes are exempt. And it can be inferred: Why do I need to teach [to teach] and the other tribes are exempt? Didn't it teach [it already taught] that tribe is liable? And since it taught [that it taught] that tribe is liable, we automatically know [we knew] that the other tribes are exempt! Rather, this teaches us [this teaches us] that it is on the ruling of its court that the other tribes are exempt, but on the ruling of the High Court - even the other tribes are liable. And they conclude: Indeed, learn from it [learn from here].

A dilemma was raised before them: One tribe that acted on the ruling of the High Court, according to Rabbi Shimon, do they bring a bull or not? Do we say that when Rabbi Shimon said to obligate each and every congregation, that one tribe is called a congregation, such as when seven tribes sinned, which were a majority? But where there is no majority, they are like an individual and are exempt, for an individual who acted on the ruling of the court is exempt. Or perhaps, since he holds that one tribe is called a congregation, it makes no difference whether it is one tribe or seven; they bring a bull for each and every tribe and a bull for the court.
A dilemma was raised before them [a dilemma was raised before them, the students]: One tribe that acted on the ruling of the High Court, according to Rabbi Shimon, does it bring a bull or not?

And they propose: Come and hear [come and hear] a solution to this problem from what we learned: What do they bring? One bull; Rabbi Shimon says: Two bulls. And we clarify: What are we dealing with [what are we dealing with]? If you say [if you say] that seven tribes sinned, then in this case, do they bring two bulls? Eight bulls are needed [are needed] according to his opinion! Rather, it must be said that one tribe sinned, and in what [and in what] according to whose ruling did they sin? If you say [if you say] on the ruling of its court, behold we said that Rabbi Shimon does not accept it [does not have it, does not accept] this reasoning that the ruling of a tribal court obligates a bull! Rather, on the ruling of the High Court. It implies that he too would agree that in this case, one tribe brings a bull!

The Gemara rejects this proof: And how can one understand that this is the reference? Who, then, is the first tanna who says that they must bring one bull? If it is Rabbi Meir, that is difficult. Doesn’t he require that the majority and not just one tribe perform a transgression in order for there to be liability? If it is Rabbi Yehuda, that is also difficult, as in his opinion the rest of the tribes are also liable to bring a bull. Rather, who is the first tanna of this baraita? The first tanna is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and the reference is to a case where six tribes sinned and in terms of population they constitute a majority of the congregation, and this baraita is as it is taught in the baraita cited earlier. In that case, Rabbi Shimon holds that two bulls are brought, one by the congregation and one by the court. Therefore, no proof may be cited from here with regard to the opinion of Rabbi Shimon in the case of one tribe that performed a transgression on the basis of a ruling of the High Court.
Rather - What are we dealing with here? For example, where six sinned, etc., since there is some majority, it says that they bring a bull and a bull for the court.

They reject this proof: And can one understand [and can you think so], that such a case is being discussed? If so, who is the first tanna [who is the first tanna]? If [if] you say that Rabbi Meir is he, behold, according to his opinion, a majority is required [a majority of Israel is required] to sin, and one tribe that sinned does not bring a bull! If [if] it is Rabbi Yehuda, behold, according to his opinion, the other tribes also bring [also bring] bulls! Rather, who is this [whose opinion is this baraita]? It is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and when six tribes sinned and they are a majority of the congregation, and in this case Rabbi Shimon holds that they bring two bulls, one for the congregation and one for the court, and as it is taught [and as we learned in a baraita] as we explained earlier. And there is no proof from here for the question of one tribe that acted on the ruling of the court.

Rather, is it not Rabbi Shimon? - And it teaches that one tribe is liable for the ruling of the High Court. This implies that when he says one tribe is called a congregation, even if one tribe sinned, they are considered like a multitude and bring a bull and a bull for the court. And this is what Rabbi Shimon holds: that where there is a majority in terms of people and a majority in terms of tribes, they bring a bull for each tribe. But where six sinned and they are a majority, or seven and they are not a majority, since there is not a majority in terms of people and a majority in terms of tribes, they are considered like one tribe and bring one bull and a bull for the court. This is derived from what it teaches: What do they bring, etc., and the first part can only be established according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, such as when six sinned, etc., and Rabbi Shimon says two bulls, one for them and one for the court.

And they further propose: Come and hear [come and hear] a solution to the problem from our mishna: And the Rabbis say: One is never liable except for the ruling of the High Court. And we clarify: Who are [who are] these Rabbis mentioned here? If you say [if you say] Rabbi Meir, behold, according to his opinion, this reasoning is not needed, for according to him, a majority is required [a majority is required]! Rather, is it not [is it not] the opinion of Rabbi Shimon! And they conclude: Indeed, learn from it [learn from here] that according to Rabbi Shimon, one tribe that sinned on the ruling of the High Court brings a bull.
